notes:
I've written notes for all 14 verses from the pages I could read. Before I finished, the research tool hit its usage limit and wouldn't run again, even after a retry. So there are clear gaps. I couldn't open netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, any Lutheran or Pentecostal site, Calvin's full chapter, or Gill's comments on verses 13–14. Wesley's own notes on wesley.nnu.edu cut off partway through verse 6. Section 3 is thin as a result: the only Catholic and Orthodox material is second-hand, and I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.

**Main sources:**
- Guzik (Enduring Word): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-8/
- Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm
- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**vv. 1–2 (the basket of summer fruit)**
- The point is a pun. The Hebrew for "summer fruit" (*qayits*) sounds like the word for "end" (*qets*). The vision is about how final the judgment is. Guzik, citing Hubbard and Boice — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-8/
- The fruit is ripe and won't keep. In the same way, Israel's time is short. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-8/
- Ellicott: it is harvest, the end of the farming year. Israel is ripe for its final doom, which will sweep down "like a scythe." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm
- Gill: this is late fruit that would rot if kept, so it has to be eaten at once. Israel's "summer of prosperity" will give way to a hard winter. He reads "the end" as the end of the northern kingdom, its nation and its religious life. "I will not pass by them" means God will no longer overlook their sins. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm
- Pulpit: fruit-gathering was the last harvest of the year, so it fits Israel's final punishment. The old Greek and Latin translations read the word differently: as a "fowler's vessel," and as a hook for pulling down fruit. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown (JFB): the word for fruit-harvest comes from a root meaning "cutting." As ripe fruit is plucked from the tree, Israel will be plucked from its land. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/amos-8.html
- Wesley: "the end" is the end of God's patience. Israel is fully ripe and ready to be gathered. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-amos/
- Coffman: "pass by" quietly echoes the Passover, when God passed over Israel and spared them. They can't expect that now. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/amos-8.html

**v. 3 (songs turn to wailing; silent corpses)**
- Ellicott and Pulpit: the word translated "temple" can also mean "palace," and that is probably the sense here. The songs are the revellers' songs of 6:5. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm
- Gill reads it as the temple, but the one at Bethel and other idol temples, not Jerusalem. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm
- Pulpit: the Hebrew is abrupt — "many corpses… he has cast them out… Hush!" The "hush" tells people to bow under God's hand. Orelli reads it instead as the numbness of suffering too deep for words. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm
- Gill gives Jewish readings of the silence: keep quiet and don't complain against God (Kimchi), or don't count the dead out loud (Aben Ezra). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm
- Wesley: the enemy will be so cruel that people won't dare bury the dead, or will have to do it secretly. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-amos/
- Constable: the dead will be thrown out like rotten fruit. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-8.html

**v. 4 (trampling the needy)**
- Ellicott, Pulpit and JFB: the verb means "pant after," like a wild animal after its prey. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/amos-8.html
- JFB: the written Hebrew text has "the meek," meaning people who are poor and also humble in spirit. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/amos-8.html
- Gill: the poor are worked and underpaid until they die of want. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm
- Wesley: "to fail" means either driving them out or making them slaves. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-amos/

**v. 5 (New Moon, Sabbath, false scales)**
- Guzik: Israel kept the holy days outwardly but couldn't wait for them to end. Cheating in business is not a small sin. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-8/
- Ellicott: this shows the northern kingdom still kept the festivals, even if people resented them. The fake scales turned the very symbol of justice into a tool for injustice (Lev. 19:35–36; Prov. 11:1). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm
- Pulpit: the poor were cheated three ways — short measure, inflated price and light weight. Money was weighed, not counted as coins, before the exile. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm
- Gill mentions other Jewish readings: Kimchi took the "new moon" as harvest month and the "sabbath" as a week. He prefers the plain sense. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm
- Wesley: they treated times of worship as a burden. The poor were "twice oppressed": they got less and paid more. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-amos/
- Constable: profit had become their god. If you are focused on what you'll do after worship, you aren't really worshipping. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-8.html

**v. 6 (buying the poor; selling the chaff)**
- Pulpit, Coffman and Utley: the poor were forced to sell themselves into slavery to pay tiny debts, worth no more than a pair of sandals (compare 2:6). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/amos-8.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-8.html
- JFB: the "refuse" is what fell through the sieve. It was mixed into the flour sold to the poor. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/amos-8.html
- Utley: in effect the poor paid for their own exploitation, because the profits bought more slaves. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-8.html
- Clarke takes "buy the poor" as buying their labour for just enough money to clear their other debts. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/amos-8.html

**v. 7 (sworn by the Pride of Jacob)**
- What "the Pride of Jacob" means is disputed:
  - God himself, Israel's glory (Pulpit, Gill, Maurer in JFB). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm
  - Israel's spiritual privileges (Calvin, as cited in JFB). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/amos-8.html
  - Samaria, or Israel's arrogance (Constable). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-8.html
  - Israel's settled wickedness (one option in Utley). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-8.html
  - The Latin Vulgate reads it as God swearing *against* Jacob's pride. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm
- Ellicott: in 6:8 God hates the "excellency" of Jacob, the poor substitute they made for his name. Here he gives the phrase its true worth. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm
- Guzik: time never erases sin. Only Christ's atoning work covers it. Compare Hebrews 6:10: God doesn't forget his people's good works either. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-8/

**v. 8 (land heaving like the Nile)**
- Ellicott and Pulpit: the solid land will rise and sink in an earthquake, like the Nile in flood. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm
- Gill: may an earthquake be expected? He links this to the earthquake of 1:1. He also reads the flood as the Assyrian army, following the Targum (the ancient Aramaic paraphrase). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm
- Clarke allows either an earthquake or unrest among the people. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/amos-8.html
- Constable thinks it probably means trembling with fear, and may picture a long national upheaval. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-8.html
- Coffman rejects a literal earthquake and sees two rivers: Assyria's Euphrates and the Nile. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/amos-8.html

**v. 9 (sun down at noon)**
- Readers disagree here; see section 2.

**v. 10 (feasts into mourning; mourning for an only son)**
- Pulpit and Gill: sackcloth and shaved heads were mourning customs. Mourning for an only son was proverbially the worst grief. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm
- Constable: losing an only son meant losing hope for the future and support in old age. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-8.html
- Guzik links this to Zechariah 12:10: one day Israel will mourn the pierced Messiah "as for an only son." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-8/
- Matthew Henry: things will not improve "at evening time." For people who refuse to repent, the end is the worst part. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Amo/Amo_008.cfm
- Gill notes Ussher's dating of three eclipses that fell on feast days soon after Amos. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm

**v. 11 (famine of hearing the word)**
- Pulpit: Israel rejected the prophets (7:12), so revelation will be withdrawn, as it was from Saul (1 Sam. 28:6; Ps. 74:9). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm
- Constable: if we won't listen to God's word, we may lose the ability to hear it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-8.html
- Matthew Henry: Israel had plenty of prophets and probably grew sick of them, like Israel with the manna. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Amo/Amo_008.cfm
- Ellicott: neglecting the word wears down the ability to recognise it. Then the seers fall silent. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm
- Gill:
  - The famine came when the ten tribes went into captivity.
  - He applies it further to the Jews after they rejected Christ and to the seven churches of Asia.
  - Today it happens when preaching is removed or false teaching wins out.
  - He fears it could happen in his own land. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm

**v. 12 (wandering sea to sea)**
- Pulpit and JFB: "from sea to sea" means the Dead Sea or Galilee to the Mediterranean, so the whole land. The south is left out because there, at Jerusalem, true worship was found, and they refused to go there. Pulpit also sees later Jews seeking a Messiah they had rejected. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/amos-8.html
- Ellicott: they will stagger about looking for one true seer. "North" and "east" were where Israel looked to pagan fortune-telling. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm
- Gill: they will look for preaching and prophets to explain the word, and find none. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm

**v. 13 (young people faint from thirst)**
- Pulpit and JFB: if even the young and strong faint, the weak will fare worse. The thirst is both spiritual and physical. Pulpit says the Hebrew "faint" literally means "be veiled," like a dimming of sight. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/amos-8.html
- Ellicott: it is especially sad when young people fall into unbelief. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm
- Utley: even the young and strong will not be able to find God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/amos-8.html

**v. 14 (swearing by Samaria, Dan and Beersheba)**
- Pulpit:
  - The "sin of Samaria" is the golden calf at Bethel; the god of Dan is the other calf, in the far north.
  - The "way of Beersheba" is the form of worship practised there.
  - Some take it as the pilgrimage road, comparing Muslims swearing by the Mecca pilgrimage. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm
- Ellicott: the "sin of Samaria" is the calf (Hos. 8:5). The "way of Beersheba" is its ritual, probably standing for Baal. He records but doesn't take the view that it refers to Asherah worship. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm
- Constable sees a play on the name of the idol Ashimah (2 Kings 17:30). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/amos-8.html
- Coffman, citing Hammershaimb: this was a god made to suit their own wishes, not the true LORD. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/amos-8.html
- Guzik: the judgment on the idolaters will be lasting. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-8/

---

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

**v. 9: figure of speech, eclipse, or the crucifixion?**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** a figure of speech for sudden punishment on people lulled by prosperity. Pressing it literally gives "gross and insipid" meanings. — https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol27/htm/iv.viii.vii.htm
- **Presbyterian (JFB):** darkness at noon is a picture of great disaster. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/amos-8.html
- **Methodist (Wesley):** Israel's "sun" set at noon in the coups and civil wars of Shallum, Menahem, Pekah and Hoshea, before the full darkness of the Assyrian invasions. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/8-9.html
- **Methodist (Clarke):** either the darkness that comes with earthquakes, or an eclipse. Ussher dated two eclipses soon after Amos. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/8-9.html
- **Anglican-leaning older commentators:** they read it mainly as a figure, perhaps prompted by a remembered eclipse.
  - Ellicott: the total eclipse of 784 BC. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm
  - Pulpit: a sudden reversal such as Pekah's fall. It doubts a plain eclipse prediction, following Pusey. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm
- **Baptist (Gill):** many church fathers applied it to the darkness at Christ's crucifixion, but Gill thinks the main meaning is the fall of Israel's kingdom. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm
- **Calvary Chapel (Chuck Smith):**
  - In his commentary, it "could be" a prophecy of the darkness at the crucifixion. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/8-9.html
  - In his sermon notes, he links it directly to the darkness at noon on the day Jesus died. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Amo/Amo_7.cfm
- **Churches of Christ (Coffman):** "an undeniable reference" to the crucifixion. He rejects the eclipse theory. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/8-9.html
- **Guzik:** many see the final Day of the LORD here. Others, such as Hubbard, see an eclipse. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-8/

**v. 11: who causes the "famine"?**
- **Withdrawal:** Gill, Pulpit, Matthew Henry and Constable say God takes away prophets and preaching. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/8.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Amo/Amo_008.cfm
- **Deafness:** Guzik, following G. Campbell Morgan, says the problem is in the hearers. The people have become unable to hear, rather than God holding back his word. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-8/
- **Both:** Ellicott says neglect first dulls hearing, and then revelation is withdrawn. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/8.htm

---

## 3. Other views (limited)

- **Modern translation:** the NET Bible renders v. 11 as "an end to divine revelation," per the parallel versions on Bible Hub. I couldn't read the NET notes themselves. — https://biblehub.com/amos/8-11.htm
- **Early church (second-hand only):**
  - The church fathers read v. 9 as the crucifixion darkness (according to Gill and Pulpit). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm
  - Barnes quotes Chrysostom (an Eastern church father, important in Orthodoxy): to mourners, even the sun at noon seems dim. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/8-9.html
  - Jerome (Catholic tradition): the Latin Vulgate has a hook for gathering fruit in v. 1. Jerome explains it as God pulling the time of captivity closer. On v. 7, he comments on God "swearing." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/8.htm
- **Ancient Greek translation (Septuagint):** v. 12 reads "the waters shall be troubled from sea to sea." — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brl/amos/8-11.html
